fallbacks.topic: Why no national flag in the world uses the color purple
fallbacks.title: Why No Flag Uses Purple #shorts
sources: Smithsonian Magazine, 'The History of Tyrian Purple Dye'

lines.text: Have you ever noticed that almost no national flag in the world uses the color purple?
It isn't because world leaders hated the color.
Until the mid-nineteenth century, purple dye was made exclusively from the slime of thousands of sea snails.
It took ten thousand snails to produce just a single gram of purple dye,
making it literally worth more than its weight in pure gold.
Only royalty could afford purple clothes, and no country could afford a purple flag.
Today, synthetic dye is cheap, but flags kept their traditional colors.

lines.text: Did you know there is only one country with a modern assault rifle on its flag?
The national flag of Mozambique features an AK-47 crossed with a farm hoe.
The rifle represents defense and the bloody struggle for national independence in 1975.
The hoe represents the country's hardworking agriculture.
They sit over an open book, symbolizing the vital importance of education.
Several political debates have tried to remove the weapon from the flag,
but citizens voted to keep it as a reminder of their hard-fought freedom.

lines.text: As you get closer, extreme gravity pulls much harder on your feet than your head.

They would see you freeze at the edge of the event horizon, slowly fading away.

lines.text: First, Hollywood lied: you cannot sink completely underwater in quicksand.
Humans have a lower density than quicksand, so you will naturally float at waist level.

Quicksand is a non-Newtonian fluid: violent movements pack the sand grains tightly around your legs.

fallbacks.topic: Why glass is actually neither a standard solid nor a liquid
fallbacks.title: Why Glass Is Not A Normal Solid #shorts
sources: American Ceramic Society, 'The Atomic Structure of Amorphous Solids'
Scientific American, 'Is Glass Liquid or Solid?'

lines.text: Why do physicists say that glass is not actually a normal solid?
In a true solid like ice or metal, atoms lock into neat, rigid crystal grids.
In a liquid, atoms move and tumble around freely.
When molten glass cools, it cools so quickly that atoms freeze in place before forming a crystal.
Its atoms are completely scrambled and disordered, exactly like a liquid frozen in time.
Scientists call this bizarre state an amorphous solid.
It has the stiffness of a solid, but the atomic chaos of a liquid.

fallbacks.topic: The acoustic engineering behind the ancient Greek Brazen Bull
fallbacks.title: The Dark Physics Of The Brazen Bull #shorts
sources: Cambridge Classical Journal, 'Perillos of Athens and the Sicilian Tyranny'

lines.text: How did ancient Greek engineers design the terrifying Brazen Bull?
Cast entirely from hollow bronze in sixth-century BC Sicily,
the device contained an intricate acoustic pipe system inside the nostrils.
When a fire was stoked beneath the belly, superheated bronze transferred heat directly inward by conduction.
As the victim inside screamed for air, the sound waves were forced through tuned brass tubes.
This modulated the human voice so it sounded from the outside like the bellowing of an enraged bull.

fallbacks.topic: Why the guillotine was originally invented as a humane medical machine
fallbacks.title: Why The Guillotine Was Called Humane #shorts
sources: Archives Nationales de France, 'Reforme des peines criminelles'

lines.text: Why was the French guillotine originally considered a humane medical breakthrough?
Before 1789, French executions were brutal, slow, and depended on the executioner's manual aim.
Dr. Joseph-Ignace Guillotin, a respected physician, proposed a mechanical solution.
He designed an angled steel blade falling from twelve feet along greased vertical grooves.
The oblique angle sliced through tissue in less than one fiftieth of a second,
eliminating botched blows and ensuring instant, painless cessation of brain function.
What was meant as an egalitarian reform ironically became the symbol of the Reign of Terror.
